name: Carlos Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach maths at Hollins Park, a big state secondary school with about fourteen hundred kids, on the edge of the city. I'm in by quarter to eight, I teach five lessons most days, from eleven-year-olds doing fractions up to seventeen-year-olds doing calculus. I've got a Year 9 form group too, so I start the day sorting out lost ties and lunch money. The best bit is the moment a kid who swore they were 'bad at maths' gets a quadratic right on the board.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marking and data, honestly. Before I started using AI tools, I'd spend Sunday evenings putting test scores into spreadsheets for the head of department, Ruth. Now I get an AI to draft the feedback sheets and I check them, which saves me maybe four hours a week. What still drains me is behaviour: one rough lesson with Year 10 on a Friday afternoon can flatten me for the whole weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staffroom: these tools are handy, use them for the boring stuff and don't expect miracles. I'd probably post something slightly smug, like 'told you so', in the maths teachers' group chat. Half of them never believed it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I like the tools, and I'd hoped they'd get good enough to really help kids who are behind. If nothing radical changes, my job looks safe, because there's a shortage of maths teachers and that won't fix itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do now: AI drafts my worksheets and feedback, I check them and teach. I'd keep putting £200 a month into savings, because Priya and I want a deposit for a flat in about three years. I'd probably apply for the second-in-department job when it comes up next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. Teaching's tiring, but it's steady, and the pay goes up a notch every year. The worry in that world would be my energy, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Priya and a deposit. What's the money picture like right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my partner, is a pharmacist, so between us we're fine but not flush. We've got about four months of costs saved, and rent on our place takes a third of what we earn. The deposit fund is the thing we guard, and in that world we'd just keep feeding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague, if any, would you worry about even in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gareth, who teaches computing, because the school keeps cutting his timetable whatever happens with AI. In a hype world, nobody's going to suddenly invest in computing teachers. The maths teacher shortage protects me in a way it doesn't protect my colleague who teaches computing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to get ahead of it, and I'd offer to run a training session on using AI for planning and marking. Online I'd be measured, something like 'it changes the job, it doesn't end it'. I wouldn't want to sound like a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think schools would use it as an excuse not to replace staff. Planning, marking, reports and parent emails are maybe a third of my week, and if software does those, the head will want me teaching more classes for the same pay. The maths shortage helps, but I'd expect fewer new hires and bigger timetables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd become the person in the department who knows these tools best, because that's the person they keep. I'd do a short course in data and AI in education, the kind the council runs online for about £300. I'd also add a bit more to savings, maybe £300 a month, in case my hours or the deposit plan wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more alert than scared. I like change, and I'd probably enjoy being the one who figures it out. What bugs me is the thought of working harder for the same money while the software gets the credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the head would want more classes. Can you picture that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it'd be in the June timetable meeting with Ruth, my head of department. My marking's automated now, so the head of department hands me an extra Year 8 set. That's how workload creeps in schools: nobody announces it. I'd say yes, because saying no looks like you're not a team player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Hollins Park in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team, first. Sandra in the exams office does all the entries and timetables by hand, and that's exactly the sort of work software eats. And the teaching assistants, because AI tutoring apps could look like a cheaper way to help the kids who are behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd try to be the calm voice: schools aren't only about teaching facts, they look after kids, and that doesn't vanish in two years. I'd probably say we need a plan from the government, fast. I'd be careful not to panic the Year 11s, who'd be scared enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if AI can do any thinking work as well as me, then explaining maths is something it does better and cheaper by 2028. What's left is the room: keeping thirty teenagers safe, calm and working, and robots can't do that until around 2031. So I think teaching becomes supervision, with fewer of us on lower pay, and I could be one of the ones cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop saving for the deposit and treat the fund as an emergency cushion; buying a flat on a teacher's pay with that ahead would be mad. I'd look at the parts of the job that are about people, like pastoral work and safeguarding, and push to move into a head of year role. I'd also start tutoring kids face to face at weekends, because parents might pay for a real person when everything else is a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the teacher who likes new tech, and that makes AGI by 2028 worse. I'd feel like I'd helped build the thing that pushes me out. I can see exactly how good it would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pause the deposit. How would that conversation with Priya go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my partner, would be calmer than me, because pharmacy has a hands-on side and legal rules about who hands out medicine. I think she'd say, 'Fine, we wait two years and see.' The hard bit would be admitting I'm the riskier earner now, when I always thought teaching was the safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What does the extra three years before robots actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the classroom still needs a human body until about 2031, so I'd have work, just a different kind. I'd be the adult in the room while an AI teaches, more like a youth worker than a maths teacher. That buys me three years to retrain into something with people at the centre, maybe educational psychology.

The **government needs a plan** fast, and I wouldn't want to panic the Year 11s.

fieldNote: His enthusiasm for AI turns into **sharper fear**, because he knows what it can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is long enough to do it properly, so let's not waste it. At work I'd push for the school to have an actual plan: what teachers do when AI can explain anything. I'd say it out loud in staff meetings, even if people rolled their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the two-year one, my explaining work goes first and the supervising work later, around 2034 when robots come. Five years means I'd be 32 when AGI arrives, which is young enough to switch properly. I still think there'll be fewer teachers, but I'd have time to not be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a part-time master's in educational psychology, about £9,000 over two years, paid partly from savings and partly from tutoring. I'd keep the deposit fund but buy somewhere smaller and cheaper, maybe a one-bed rather than the two-bed we planned. And I'd use AI every day to see what it can't do yet, because that tells me where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which is better than the fast one. There's a bit of excitement too. I'd be working towards something rather than waiting to be told my post is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: £9,000 is a lot from four months of savings. What gets cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer trip to see my brother in Lisbon goes first, and probably the car; I can cycle to Hollins Park. Priya and I would eat out once a month instead of every week. None of that hurts much at 27, which is the one advantage of not having kids yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the school would rather supervise than teach. Would you stay to the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd stay while I study, because the pay and the pension matter. Fifty teachers would be applying for the same few jobs after the cuts. I'd want to leave Hollins Park before the school makes cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, and that teaching unions and the government should use it to redesign what school is for. Online I'd probably write a long post about it, which nobody would read. I'd say teachers who learn the tools now will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I would be fine, more or less. By 2036 I'm 37, and I could be a head of year, a psychologist, or running the school's AI side. Robots in the classroom around 2039 is so far off that I'd have changed jobs twice by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead and buy the two-bed flat with Priya in about three years, as planned. I'd go for the second-in-department job and then aim to lead how the school uses AI, maybe as an assistant head by my mid-thirties. And I'd start the psychology course later, maybe in five years, once I know which way things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's on my mind, and I'd be watching every new release, but it's not keeping me up. I'd feel like I had time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd 'probably' be fine. What's the part that isn't fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids. A Year 7 starting at Hollins Park in 2026 finishes school in 2033, three years before AGI, and I don't know what to tell them to study. When a kid asks me what maths is for, I used to say 'jobs'. With AGI by 2036, I'd need a new answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell that Year 7 now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell an eleven-year-old to learn maths because it trains you to think in steps and check your own work, and AI will need people who can catch its mistakes. I'd also tell them to get good at something with their hands. I'm not sure I believe the first part as much as I want to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to retrain and I'd be stuck supervising rather than teaching. What would help is the government saying clearly what schools are for in that world, and paying for teachers to retrain while still earning. A year of paid study leave would change everything for someone like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want an AI to teach my own future kids. I wouldn't, not on its own. A good teacher notices the quiet kid who's hungry or scared, and I want a person in the room doing that.

headlineQuote: A good teacher notices the quiet kid who's hungry or scared, and I want a person in the room doing that.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old maths teacher** at Hollins Park, a large state secondary on the city's edge.
He uses **AI every day** for worksheets and feedback, and expects to be the department's go-to person.
He and Priya, a pharmacist, are saving for a **flat deposit**, with about four months of costs saved.
Slower scenarios bring **workload creep** and promotion plans; the fast one makes him fear becoming a supervisor.
His pragmatic answer to every scenario is to **move early**, before cuts flood the market with teachers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because there's no time to retrain before teaching becomes supervision.
whatWouldHelp: A clear national answer on **what schools are for** once AI can teach.
